questions.q: What is RPC, a remote procedure call?
questions.explain: With RPC you think in functions, not URLs: tasks.call("tasks.count", { userId }) runs code in the task service and returns its result. It is most useful between your own services.
options: A way to send HTML pages from one server to another
Calling a function by name that runs in another process, and getting its result back
A database query that runs in parallel
A browser API for calling JavaScript from HTML

questions.q: In @zudojs/rpc, what does the transport do?
questions.explain: A procedure is the function on the far side, the server holds the procedures, the client builds requests, and the transport carries them, for example over HTTP.
options: It holds the procedures and runs the right one
It checks each payload against the schema
It carries the request frame to the server and the answer back

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A procedure name is dot-separated words, like tasks.create. A name with a space is refused when you create the procedure, long before anyone calls it.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Two procedures with the same name would make calls ambiguous, so the second register throws. Nothing is silently replaced.

questions.q: A procedure is created with { input: NewTask }, a schema. When does the schema run?
questions.explain: The server checks every payload against the input schema first. A payload that fails never reaches your handler, and a payload that passes arrives cleaned, for example with the title trimmed.
options: After the handler, on the result
On every payload, before the handler runs; the handler receives the value the schema produced
Only when the client asks for validation

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The response carries the same id as the request, so the caller knows which answer belongs to which question. The handler received the value the schema produced, so the title was trimmed.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: handle never throws for a bad request. An unknown procedure comes back as a response with success: false and an error, so one bad call cannot crash the server.

questions.q: What is the smallest thing that works as an RPCTransport?
questions.explain: Any object with send(request) works. The package ships ready-made ones, createRPCMemoryTransport(server) and createRPCHttpTransport({ url }), and the retry example wraps one in a small object of its own.
options: An object with a send(request) method that returns the response

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The client turns each response into a normal return value. The first task got id 1, and the list holds both titles. The transport here is just an object with send that calls the server in the same process.

questions.q: You write client.call<{ id: number }, Task>("tasks.get", { id: 1 }). What does the Task type guarantee at runtime?
questions.explain: Types disappear when the code runs. The other service could send anything. Treat its answer like any other outside data.
options: The client checks that the answer is a Task
Nothing: it only tells TypeScript what you expect; validate the answer with a schema if it matters
The server refuses to answer anything else
The transport converts the answer into a Task

questions.q: The billing service calling your task service is also yours. Should the task service validate its payloads?
questions.explain: The other service can have bugs, old versions or be compromised. An input schema stops a payload like { id: "1; DROP TABLE tasks" } before it reaches the handler.
options: No, your own services can be trusted
Yes: a payload comes from another program, so it is untrusted, even when that program is yours
Only for procedures that write data
Only when the call goes over HTTP

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The title is too short, so the schema rejected the payload and the handler never ran. The client throws, and details lists every problem with its path so the caller can fix the request.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The handler threw an RPCError with expose: true, so its code and message reach the caller unchanged. That is how you send a deliberate, safe error message.
options: TASK_NOT_FOUND - The server encountered an internal error while handling this request.

questions.q: A handler crashes with an ordinary error. What does this print?
questions.explain: The real message contains a host and a port that an outsider must never see. The caller gets a fixed message, and the real error goes to onInternalError, where you log it.
options:
[server log] connect ECONNREFUSED 10.0.0.5:5432
[caller] The server encountered an internal error while handling this request.
[caller] The server encountered an internal error while handling this request.

questions.q: A handler throws a NotFoundError from @zudojs/errors. What does this print?
questions.explain: A NotFoundError is meant for the caller (its expose flag is true), so its message arrives under the matching code, RPC_NOT_FOUND. An ordinary error, with no expose, would become RPC_INTERNAL_ERROR with the fixed message.
options: RPC_INTERNAL_ERROR - The server encountered an internal error while handling this request.
NOT_FOUND - The server encountered an internal error while handling this request.

questions.q: The memory transport copies each frame through JSON, as a network would. What does this print?
questions.explain: With plain JSON, the default, the Date became a string, the Set became an empty object, and the undefined field disappeared, all without an error. Design results as plain JSON: ISO strings, arrays and null.
options: { dueAt: 2026-10-01T09:00:00.000Z, tags: Set(2) { 'home', 'shopping' }, note: undefined, count: 2 }

questions.q: A procedure returns a due date and a set of tags. What is the safest result shape?
questions.explain: Results travel as JSON. Dates as ISO strings and sets as arrays arrive exactly as sent, and even programs not written in JavaScript can read them. When both sides are your own TypeScript code, createRPCJsonSerializer({ preserveTypes: true }) on both ends keeps richer types.
options: { dueAt: new Date(...), tags: new Set([...]) }

questions.q: A frame's metadata says { userId: "admin" }. Can the handler trust it?
questions.explain: Metadata is useful for request ids and trace ids, but never for deciding who the caller is. Identity that your code verified (for example after checking a token) goes in handle(frame, { auth }).
options: Yes, metadata is signed by the client
Yes, if the call came over HTTPS
No: the caller writes metadata, so it can put anything there; use verified identity from context.auth
Only when the id is a UUID

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first call only claimed to be admin in its metadata, and nothing verified that, so the middleware refused it. The second call had a verified identity, and the handler used ada.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The middleware only reads context.auth. Bo's metadata claims role: "admin", but his verified role is user, so he is refused. Ada's verified role is admin.

questions.q: RPC middleware works like HTTP middleware. What does this print?
questions.explain: Each middleware gets next(). Code before await next() runs on the way in, in order. Code after it runs on the way out, once the handler and the inner middleware are done.
options: outer before > inner > handler > outer after
outer before > outer after > inner > handler
handler > inner > outer before > outer after
inner > outer before > handler > outer after

questions.q: Why does the fetch handler's auth option compare the token with timingSafeEqualString instead of ===?
questions.explain: A constant-time comparison takes the same time whether the first or the last character is wrong, so the timing reveals nothing about the secret.
options: === does not work on long strings
=== stops at the first different character, and an attacker can measure that time to guess the token one character at a time

questions.q: Two real services must share the RPC token. How should they get it?
questions.explain: Secrets never go in source code. Each side reads TASKS_RPC_TOKEN from the environment, and a service that finds it missing or shorter than 32 characters stops at startup instead of running unprotected.
options: Write it in the source code of both services
Create a random token at startup on each side
Both read it from an environment variable, and the service refuses to start without a strong one
Send it in the first RPC call's metadata

questions.q: The HTTP transport's fetch option hands each request straight to the fetch handler, so no real server is needed. A caller sends a guessed token. What does this print?
questions.explain: Throwing RPCAuthenticationError in auth refuses the call before any procedure runs. The handler answers with an RPC error frame, and the client rebuilds it as a typed RPCAuthenticationError. Any other error thrown in auth would be answered as an internal error.

questions.q: Someone posts a plain-text body to the RPC endpoint, as an HTML form or a curious visitor might. What does this print?
questions.explain: The fetch handler refuses anything that is not a JSON POST, limits the body size (1 MiB by default), and answers every failure with an RPC error frame, never an HTML page or a stack trace.

questions.q: A call through createRPCHttpTransport times out on the client. What happens on the server?
questions.explain: The HTTP transport passes cancellation along. The server stops working for a caller that has left, as long as the handler looks at context.signal or passes it on.
options: Nothing: the procedure always runs to the end
The transport aborts the fetch, and the fetch handler aborts the procedure's context.signal, so a handler that checks it can stop
The server kills the handler by force

questions.q: A procedure has a timeout and its handler loops through slow steps. What must the handler do so it really stops?
questions.explain: A timeout does not stop a handler by force. The server aborts context.signal, and the handler must look at it, or pass it on to fetch and database calls.
options: Nothing; the server kills the handler when time runs out
Check context.signal.aborted between steps and return early
Catch the timeout error and rethrow it

questions.q: When does a caller need to send a deadline in metadata.deadline?
questions.explain: createRPCMemoryTransport and createRPCHttpTransport carry a timeout or an abort to the server, which aborts context.signal. A hand-written transport may not, so the caller sends a point in time instead, and the server stops by then, never later.
options: Always, or the built-in transports never cancel the server
Only with a transport you wrote yourself that cannot cancel the far side; the built-in transports already cancel the server when the caller gives up
Only to cache the result until the deadline
Only to retry the call at the deadline

questions.q: Which error is worth retrying?
questions.explain: Only retry errors that can go away. A validation or permission error fails the same way every time, so retrying only adds load.
options: A validation error for a title that is too short
A forbidden error for a user who is not an admin

questions.q: A tasks.create call timed out. Is it safe to retry it automatically?
questions.explain: Only retry calls that are safe to repeat, like reading a list. idempotent: true on a procedure documents that; the package does not retry anything by itself.
options: Not by default: the first call may have worked on the server, and a retry could create a second task
Yes, because the package removes duplicates
No, timed-out calls can never be retried

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: With exponential backoff the wait doubles after each failure: 10 ms, then 20 ms. The third attempt worked, so retry returned its result and did not use the fourth.
options:
attempt 1: wait 10 ms
attempt 2: wait 20 ms
tasks 3

attempt 1: wait 10 ms
attempt 2: wait 10 ms
tasks 3

attempt 1: wait 10 ms
attempt 2: wait 20 ms
attempt 3: wait 40 ms
tasks 4

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: retryIf says only unavailable errors are worth another try. This error is not one, so retry gives up at once and throws the original error.
options: gave up after 1 call(s): Title is too short
gave up after 4 call(s): Title is too short
gave up after 3 call(s): Title is too short
gave up after 1 call(s): retry failed

questions.q: The lesson uses jitter: "none". What should you use in production, and why?
questions.explain: If a thousand clients all retry after exactly 100 ms, they hit the service together and knock it down again. Random jitter spreads them out. The example only turns it off so its output is the same every run.
options: The default random jitter, so many clients do not all hit a recovering service at the same moment

questions.q: Build a tiny RPC server by hand. Finish handle(frame): look up frame.procedure in procedures. If it exists, return { id, success: true, result } with the handler's result. If not, return { id, success: false, error: "not found" }. Never throw. The program should print the two lines in the comments.
questions.explain: This is the core of an RPC server: find the procedure by name, run it, and answer with the request's id. An unknown name becomes an answer with success: false, never a crash.
questions.expected:
{ id: 'r1', success: true, result: 2 }
{ id: 'r2', success: false, error: 'not found' }

questions.q: Finish toWire(error), which turns a thrown error into what the caller may see. If error.expose is true, return { code: error.code, message: error.message }. Otherwise return { code: "INTERNAL", message: "Something went wrong." } and never the real message. The program should print the two lines in the comments.
questions.explain: Hiding is the default; showing is the exception you opt into. The crash's message names a host and a port, so it must stay on the server, in the logs.
questions.expected:
{ code: 'TASK_NOT_FOUND', message: 'Task 7 not found' }
{ code: 'INTERNAL', message: 'Something went wrong.' }

questions.q: Make a result safe for the wire. Finish toPlain(summary): return an object where dueAt is an ISO string, tags is an array, and note is null when it is undefined. The program should print the line in the comment.
questions.explain: ISO strings, arrays and null are plain JSON, so they arrive exactly as sent. Without this, the date would become a string anyway, the Set an empty object, and note would vanish.

questions.q: Write the check a requireUser middleware makes. Finish callerId(context): return context.auth.userId when it is a string, and throw an Error with the message Sign in first. otherwise. Never read context.metadata. The program should print the two lines in the comments.
questions.explain: Use optional chaining, context.auth?.userId, because an anonymous call has no auth. Metadata is written by the caller, so a claim of admin there changes nothing.

questions.q: Finish shouldRetry(error, idempotent) for a retry helper. Return true only when the error's name is "Unavailable" or "Timeout" and the call is idempotent. The program should print true false false.
questions.explain: Both rules must hold: the error can go away, and repeating the call is safe. A timed-out tasks.create may already have created the task, so it is not retried. A validation error fails the same way every time.

questions.q: Finish waits(delay, failures, backoff): return the list of waits before each retry. With "exponential" the wait doubles each time; with "linear" it grows by delay each time. The program should print [ 100, 200, 400 ] and then [ 100, 200, 300 ].
questions.explain: Exponential backoff is delay * 2 ** (attempt - 1): 100, 200, 400. Linear is delay * attempt: 100, 200, 300. Growing waits give a struggling service time to recover.

questions.q: Finish sameToken(a, b), a comparison that does not stop at the first difference. If the lengths differ, return false. Otherwise look at every character: combine the differences of charCodeAt with |= and ^, and return whether the total is 0. The program should print true false false.
questions.explain: ^ is 0 only for equal characters, and |= keeps any difference. The loop always runs to the end, so the time does not reveal where the first wrong character is. In real code, use timingSafeEqualString from @zudojs/crypto.

questions.q: A body that is valid JSON but not a frame reaches handle. What does this print?
questions.explain: handle checks the frame's shape itself and answers with success: false for anything malformed. That is why the fetch handler can pass it whatever JSON arrives.

questions.q: The service starts without the variable set. What does this print?
questions.explain: A missing variable is undefined, so !token is true. Refusing to start is better than running an RPC endpoint with no protection or a weak token.
options: TASKS_RPC_TOKEN is missing or too short. Refusing to start.

questions.q: The service never comes back. What does this print?
questions.explain: attempts: 3 means three calls in total. When the last one fails too, retry throws the last error, so the caller can still tell what went wrong.

questions.q: Each step takes 50 ms and the client gives up after 75 ms, first through the memory transport, then through a hand-written one. What does this print?
questions.explain: Both callers got RPC_TIMEOUT at 75 ms. The memory transport carried the cancel to the server, so the handler stopped after step 2. The hand-written transport only calls server.handle(request), so the server never heard about it and worked for nobody. That is the case metadata.deadline is for.
options:
RPC_TIMEOUT
stopped at step 2
RPC_TIMEOUT
ran all 5 steps

RPC_TIMEOUT
stopped at step 2

stopped at step 2
